reading3.title: A different newspaper round
reading3.text:
When Felix wanted to earn some money, he asked for a Saturday job at a small shop. The owner needed someone to deliver newspapers. Felix liked the idea because he knew the streets nearby and could work before football practice.
On his first morning, he put the newspapers in the order of the houses on his list. However, a road was closed, and he had to go a different way. He became worried about being late. Instead of cycling faster, he stopped and changed the order of the last few deliveries.
At one house, an older customer asked him to put the newspaper through the side door because she found it difficult to bend down. Felix wrote a short note beside her address. He then checked the rest of his list for special instructions.
The next Saturday was much easier. He arrived at the shop ten minutes early to read the list before setting off. He still finished in time for football. The owner was pleased that Felix had learnt to plan his work and listen to customers, rather than simply hurry.

reading3.title: The bread before breakfast
reading3.text:
Iris usually saw the lights of a bakery on her way to school. She wanted to know what happened inside so early, so she arranged to spend one morning there for a school project. She expected the hardest job to be carrying heavy bags of flour.
The baker asked her to arrive at five. When she entered, some bread was already in the oven. He explained that the work had begun much earlier. First, Iris helped put bread on shelves. Each type had a different place, and she had to look carefully at the labels.
A customer arrived for an order of twenty rolls. Iris put them in a bag, but the baker asked her to count them again. She had included two more than the order. He said working accurately was important, even when people were waiting.
Back at school, Iris wrote about the visit. Her classmates were most interested in the early start, but she wrote that remembering many small jobs was the real challenge. She enjoyed the warm, friendly shop, although she decided she would prefer a job that started after breakfast.

reading3.title: The school sound team
reading3.text:
Noah wanted to act in the school play, but there were no speaking parts left. The drama teacher suggested helping with sound instead. Noah was disappointed because he thought pressing buttons would be boring. He agreed to try for one week.
During the first practice, he learnt that every sound had to happen at the right moment. He wrote notes beside the actors' words in a copy of the play. One sound was a door closing. He recorded a real door at home because the sound on the computer did not match the small room in the story.
On the day of the show, a speaker stopped working. Noah told the teacher immediately. Together they moved the other speaker nearer the middle of the hall and tested it before the audience came in.
After the play, several parents said the sound had helped them imagine the different places. Noah felt proud. He still wanted to act one day, but he understood that people the audience could not see were important too. He offered to teach another pupil what he had learnt.

reading3.text:
When Tara's phone needed repairing, she had to spend a weekend without it. At first she was annoyed. She had planned to watch videos and message her friends. Her mother suggested writing a list of other things she might enjoy, rather than waiting for the phone to return.
On Saturday morning, Tara found an unfinished jigsaw puzzle in a cupboard. Her younger brother joined her, and they talked while looking for pieces. In the afternoon, she visited a friend. They had not arranged it online, so Tara phoned the friend's house first to check she was there.
On Sunday, Tara took a notebook to the park and drew people walking their dogs. Her pictures were not very good, but she liked watching carefully. She noticed a small pond she had passed many times without seeing.
When she collected her phone on Monday, she was glad to have it back. However, she turned off some messages that often interrupted her homework. She did not decide to stop using her phone. She simply wanted to choose when to use it.

George noticed that people often threw away small things that might be repaired. He could mend a loose button, but he did not know much about other repairs. A local community centre invited him to help at a monthly repair afternoon.
His first job was welcoming visitors and writing down what they had brought. The adults did the difficult repairs. George watched them and asked questions when they were not busy. He learnt how to find a broken wire in a lamp, although he was not allowed to repair electrical items himself.
One visitor brought a wooden toy with a wheel missing. George found a spare wheel in a box and asked an adult to help attach it. The visitor had played with the toy as a child and was pleased to keep it for her grandson.
The afternoons changed how George looked at old things. He still knew that not everything could be saved. Now, though, he checked whether someone could repair an item before putting it in the rubbish. He also learnt that asking for help was part of learning a practical skill.

reading3.title: A place on the school radio
reading3.text:
Lily enjoyed listening to the school radio but thought she was too shy to speak on it. When the radio team needed someone to prepare short interviews, she volunteered to write questions. She was comfortable talking to one person, even if speaking to a large group frightened her.
Her first guest was a student who had won a drawing prize. Lily prepared ten questions, but the interview became more interesting when she listened to an unexpected answer. The guest mentioned learning from his grandmother. Lily asked about her instead of moving straight to the next question.
Later, the team asked Lily to record the introduction. She practised several times in an empty classroom. Hearing her own voice felt strange, but she realised that speaking clearly mattered more than sounding like a professional presenter.
The programme received friendly comments. Lily still felt nervous before recording, but she no longer saw that as a reason to stop. For the next interview, she prepared fewer questions and left more space to listen. She hoped other quiet students would try joining the team too.

reading3.title: Learning to wait
reading3.text:
Chloe joined a nature club because she wanted to photograph wild birds. On the first walk, she kept moving to get nearer them. Each time, the birds flew away. The club leader suggested choosing one place and waiting quietly.
Chloe found that difficult. She could see other people taking pictures while her camera stayed in its bag. The leader asked her to spend five minutes just watching. She noticed which branches the birds used and where the light fell through the leaves.
A small bird finally landed close enough for a picture. Chloe lifted her camera slowly and took one photograph. It was not perfect: a leaf covered part of the bird. However, she liked it more than the many distant pictures she had taken before.
At the next meeting, the group discussed their photographs. Chloe explained what she had learnt about waiting. She wanted to return to the same spot at a different time of day. Instead of trying to collect as many pictures as possible, she now enjoyed understanding the place and the animals in it.

reading3.title: The school lunch survey
reading3.text:
James heard friends complain about the school lunches. Some wanted different food, while others said the queue was too long. He suggested a survey, but the head teacher asked him to make the questions fair rather than collect only complaints.
With two classmates, James wrote questions about choice, price and waiting time. They tested the form on a small group first. One question confused people, so they changed its wording before giving the survey to other classes.
The results surprised them. Most students liked the food, but many missed the start of lunchtime activities because they waited so long. The kitchen manager explained that everyone arrived at once. The students suggested letting different year groups come five minutes apart.
The school tried the new system for two weeks. The queue became shorter, and the team asked students for comments again. James had hoped for more food choices, but he was glad they had found a practical change. He learnt that useful answers sometimes lead to a different solution from the one you first imagined.

reading3.title: The bag that travelled twice
reading3.text:
Opal bought a second-hand travel bag for a short visit to her cousin. It had a small pocket she did not notice until she was packing. Inside was a photograph and a note from someone thanking the previous owner for a lovely holiday.
Opal thought the photograph might be important. There was no full address, but the second-hand shop remembered who had donated the bag. A shop worker offered to contact the family without giving Opal their private details.
Two days later, a woman came to collect the photograph. It showed her father on a family trip many years before. She had searched for it after giving away his old things. She thanked Opal and told her a little about the journey in the picture.
When Opal finally used the bag, she put her own ticket in the pocket. She checked it carefully before unpacking at home. The experience made her think about the stories behind ordinary objects. She still liked finding cheap things in second-hand shops, but now she also looked at them with more curiosity.

speaking.part2_prompt: These pictures show family activities. Do you like these different things? Say why or why not.
speaking.examiner_script:
Mock 10.
These pictures show family activities. Do you like these different things? Say why or why not. Talk together.
Allow the pair to exchange ideas for about 1-2 minutes. If necessary, ask about an unused picture: What about doing a puzzle?
Then invite each candidate to say which they prefer and why. Ask follow-up questions about whether one option is fun, useful, easy, expensive or interesting, choosing words that fit the activity.
Phase 2 questions to both candidates:
Do you prefer staying at home or going out with family? Why?
Is it important for families to make plans together? Why?
Thank you. That is the end of the test.

Illustrative exchange, not a script for candidates to memorise:
Candidate A: I enjoy walking by the sea because it helps me relax. What do you think?
Candidate B: I prefer making dinner. I can do it with my family.
Candidate A: That sounds good. Do you do it often?
Candidate B: Sometimes at weekends. How about you?
Accept different opinions and reasons. Assess language and interaction rather than agreement.
